est-mcneill-speed-musk.nombre: The impossible speed of Elon Musk
est-mcneill-speed-musk.texto:
# The impossible speed of Elon Musk — Jon McNeill on The Knowledge Project

*Jon McNeill, Tesla's president during its 10x years, talking with Shane Parrish (Nov 10, 2026, 1 h 46 min). You already read his book* The Algorithm *(★5, Oct 15); this note covers what the interview adds beyond it: the habits that make an organization fast.*

## Think about this first
*Through your own lens, before reading on — nobody grades it.* Where in your work right now (Exo, the Grupo Ferra work, your classes) does an answer or a piece of bad news take days to reach the person who needs it — and what would make it reach them the same day?

## The 80/20

**Musk's bet is that speed of every kind compounds into an advantage that lasts for years:** speed of decision, of cash through the business, of response, of learning. Competitors usually move slower, so each fast loop adds distance. Tesla's aluminum casting is McNeill's example: it removed about half of the car factory and, by his count, gave Tesla an eight-year lead. ▶ [Watch: the casting story, 2 min](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=3165)

**1 · Speed comes from feedback loops, not from running hot.** McNeill says the pace is not "every minute, every day." The team thinks a problem through, then "hits the speed button." The loops are concrete. Autopilot ships two or three updates a week because six months of waiting means six months of lost learning when you are already 99% sure (at 10% sure, you don't ship). Every night executives drove home a random car off the line, and engineers had their notes by 8 a.m. Musk read the X feedback and McNeill read Reddit, daily. *Action creates information; information creates certainty.* ▶ [Watch: why weekly releases, 5 min](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=1112)

**2 · Communication is shaped for speed.** The org chart's path for a question looks like a heartbeat on an EKG: up the hierarchy, then back down. Musk wanted it flat, "like a dead patient": go straight to the person who has the answer, never through their boss. Two rules followed. **Three-sentence emails:** (1) here's my problem, (2) here's what I think the solution is, (3) here's my next step, plus any resource or permission I need. **Bad news as fast as you know it**, because it only gets worse with time. Sitting on bad news was the one sure way onto Musk's bad side. ▶ [Watch: three-sentence emails, 1.5 min](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=624)

![The same question travels up and back down in most companies, straight across at Tesla](img/mcneill-speed-1.svg)

**3 · A four-step decision cheat sheet.**

| Step | The question | McNeill's example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is the end state? Does everyone agree? | An offer for one of his companies: success = a return hurdle, a valuation, a good home for it |
| 2 | What would need to be true to get there? | What has to change in the product or process |
| 3 | What will it cost to make those things true? | A rough guess is fine at first |
| 4 | Impact vs. effort, against everything else on the plate | A $100M product that costs $200M to build fails here |

What doesn't make the cut goes on a no-list, and (from Sheryl Sandberg) the no-list should be much longer than the yes-list. That no-list is your opportunity cost. For risk, his one question is: **where is the asymmetry?** Upside asymmetry → bet. Downside asymmetry → don't bet until you remove it. ▶ [Watch: the cheat sheet, 4 min](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=1417)

**4 · Product meetings open with the customer and end at a whiteboard.** Every product meeting started with Musk asking McNeill, *"What does the market want?"* For the Model X the answer was mothers asking for a bench seat for three car seats. Musk, the head of engineering and supply chain went straight to the whiteboard; junior engineers watched and learned that "the currency here is getting stuff done." No slides for product, because slides hide the problems: you show the real software or the real part. ▶ [Watch: how product meetings ran, 8 min](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=1844)

**5 · Great products start from two or three requirements that must be true.** Jobs's chief of staff told McNeill how the iPod was designed: a week in a room to fix two requirements — 1,000 songs, any song in 4 seconds — and it had to be beautiful. When engineers proposed an FM radio, Jobs asked, "Is that a thousand songs or four seconds?" Neither one, so it stayed out. A great product sells itself; Tesla grew with a marketing budget of zero. ▶ [Watch: the iPod requirements, 3 min](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=2596)

**6 · The weed whacker.** Processes are gardens that nobody weeds, so requirements stay long after anyone remembers why. Musk asked a question like "Do we really need Salesforce? Every seat is a tax on growth" almost weekly. McNeill's own exercise, borrowed from Lululemon's CEO, is **fire yourself**: once a year, list what your successor would obviously do on day one, then ask why you haven't done it.

## The words
- **Feedback loop** — the time from doing something to learning whether it worked; Tesla tries to make each loop daily or weekly.
- **Three-sentence email** — problem · proposed solution · next step (with the ask).
- **Asymmetry** — whether the possible upside of a bet is much bigger than the downside, or the reverse.
- **Battlefield promotion** — giving someone who performs a much bigger job right away, even if nobody has done that job before.
- **Dogfooding** — leaders using their own product as a customer gets it, not a polished copy.

## Connects to what you already know
- **[[the-algorithm-challenge-every-assumption_2026-10-18|The Algorithm]]** (McNeill, ★5, Oct) — *amplifies.* The book gives the five steps; the interview shows step 4 ("speed reveals the warts") working as a whole culture: weekly releases, daily dogfooding, bad news the same day. You wrote that you "don't have many processes" to apply it to. The communication rules apply to every team, including yours.
- ***The Goal*** (Goldratt, ★4, Sept) — *same root.* It's the first book McNeill gives people, and the source of your filter #1, the bottleneck. A slow feedback loop is a bottleneck on learning.
- **[[Isaacson-Elon Musk|Elon Musk]]** (Isaacson, ★4) and ***Power Play*** (Higgins, ★4) — *the other side.* Both describe the same speed from outside: the "surges," production hell, people burning out. McNeill's own exit (below) fits their account better than his book does.
- ***The 7 Habits*** (Covey, ★5) — *a surprise.* It's McNeill's second book, and his time-blocking comes straight from it.
- **Your subsidiarity filter** — *the same move, other reason.* "Go to the person who has the answer" is close to "ask the one it lands on." McNeill does it for speed; you hold it for dignity.

## Try it this week
For one week, send the people you work with three-sentence messages only — problem · proposed fix · next step and what you need. Watch which replies come back faster.

## Other ways to see it
- **The cost of shipping at 99%.** In December 2023 Tesla recalled about 2 million cars because U.S. regulators (NHTSA) found Autopilot's controls could fail to prevent driver misuse; the fix was a software update ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/12/13/tesla-recalls-nearly-all-us-vehicles-over-autopilot-system-defects)). Fast loops let you fix fast, and they also put errors in front of millions of people first.
- **The human cost, from McNeill himself.** He left because his family told him over Christmas that he had become moody and mean, and he says he wasn't able to help Musk through his mental-health struggles ([1:07:10](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=4030)). The speed culture he praises is the same place that wore him down.

Limits: everything here is one insider's memory, told by a former executive who now sells the method (his book and his firm). None of it comes with data you can check, except the recall.

Still open: is the speed a method anyone can copy, or does it depend on a founder who can, in McNeill's words, "shut off failure" and raise more capital whenever the plan needs it?

## Go further — pick a path
*Each path is already cut down: only the minutes that carry it. Skip the rest of the 1 h 46 min.*

**A · Run a faster team — ~25 min** *(how you run the Grupo Ferra work)*
1. ▶ [8:44–14:46](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=524) — culture of speed, battlefield promotions, three-sentence emails, Sandberg's weekly clear-the-air meeting (6 min)
2. ▶ [23:37–29:15](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=1417) — the decision cheat sheet and "don't wait for perfect information" (6 min)
3. ▶ [1:16:33–1:20:00](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=4593) — how he spots real talent, and the last interview used to imprint the culture (3.5 min)
4. ▶ [3 Takeaways — "Weekly Cadence and Focus," 10:49–13:35](https://youtu.be/zSRBeZBl_mM?t=649) — the same speed seen through Tesla's weekly rhythm (3 min)

**B · Build products people pull — ~25 min** *(Exo as a product)*
1. ▶ [30:44–39:23](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=1844) — product meetings that open with "what does the market want," no slides, dogfooding, the bench seat (8.5 min)
2. ▶ [39:23–46:30](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=2363) — simple requirements, the iPod's two numbers, a product that sells itself (7 min — skip the ads at 41:40–43:16)
3. ▶ [46:30–52:45](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=2790) — growing with a $0 marketing budget, mobile service (6 min)

**C · Simplify before you automate — ~30 min** *(your agents and jobs: the algorithm applied to the machinery you build)*
1. ▶ [56:36–1:07:10](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=3396) — the five steps told fresh, the ETF example, the weed whacker, "is Salesforce a tax on growth?" (10.5 min)
2. ▶ [3 Takeaways — "Manual Before Automation," 15:54–18:08](https://youtu.be/zSRBeZBl_mM?t=954) — why the last step is the last step (2 min)
3. ▶ [3 Takeaways — "Question Requirements" + "Cut Clicks and Paperwork," 2:20–4:19](https://youtu.be/zSRBeZBl_mM?t=140) (2 min)
4. Then the exercise from the 80/20: map one of your jobs on paper, circle the steps you'd pay for as its customer, delete one.

**D · The human cost — ~10 min** *(the question this note leaves open)*
1. ▶ [1:07:10–1:12:40](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=4030) — why he left Tesla, in his own words (5.5 min)
2. ▶ [1:12:40–1:14:21](https://youtu.be/pRXMqm5bMFk?t=4360) — the "fire yourself" exercise (2 min)

Sources: [the full interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pRXMqm5bMFk) (Knowledge Project, Nov 10, 2026) · [3 Takeaways with McNeill](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zSRBeZBl_mM) (19 min, Mar 2026).

est-anthropic-agents.texto:
# Building effective agents

## Think about this first

Is the Grupo Ferra assistant an agent, or a workflow with one decision in it? Write which, and why.

## The 80/20

Anthropic's note (December 2024) comes from a year of watching teams build with Claude. Its finding: the teams that shipped used simple, composable patterns, not big frameworks. It makes one distinction, gives five patterns, and ends with three rules.

**The building block.** Everything starts with an *augmented model*: one model call that can search, call tools and remember. Before adding steps, make that one call as good as it can be: a clear prompt, the right context, tools it understands.

**The distinction.** A *workflow* runs steps you wrote, in the order you wrote them; the model fills in the words. An *agent* decides its own steps, calls tools, and loops until it thinks it is done. Agents cost more, fail in new ways, and are harder to explain to a board. Use the workflow until it is clearly not enough.

**The five workflow patterns.**
1. *Prompt chaining* — one step feeds the next; check between steps. Use it when the task splits cleanly into fixed parts: draft the outline, check it, then write.
2. *Routing* — classify first, then send each case to the prompt built for it. Use it when cases are different enough that one prompt would serve none of them well: refunds, technical questions, complaints.
3. *Parallelization* — run the same job several times or split it; vote or merge. Splitting buys speed; voting buys confidence, like three reviewers looking for the same risk.
4. *Orchestrator–workers* — one model plans and hands out pieces; others do them. Use it when you can't know the pieces in advance, like a code change that touches an unknown number of files.
5. *Evaluator–optimizer* — one model drafts, another judges, loop a few times. It works when good feedback exists and a human could say clearly what to fix.

**When an agent earns its cost.** When the problem is open-ended, the number of steps can't be predicted, and you trust the model's judgment in that setting. The note's two examples are customer support with real actions (refunds, ticket updates) and coding agents, where tests tell the agent if it worked. Agents also need guardrails: a step limit, a sandbox to test in, and a human checkpoint before anything that can't be undone.

**Where Grupo Ferra sits.** Routing plus a human check: classify the stoppage, draft the report from the template for that class, the supervisor approves. No loop, no tools that write. That is why the board can understand it. Phase two could add an evaluator: a second pass that checks each draft against last month's approved reports before the supervisor sees it.

**The three rules.**
1. *Keep it simple.* Start with the simplest thing; add a step only when a measured failure demands it. Every added step is a place to explain "who answers when it is wrong".
2. *Show the planning.* When the system decides something, it should say what it decided and why, so a person can catch the mistake early.
3. *Design the tools like a product.* Anthropic spent more time on the tools than on the prompt for their coding agent. Write each tool's description as if for a new hire, give clear examples, and shape inputs so mistakes are hard to make (absolute file paths instead of relative ones).

**On frameworks.** They make the first demo fast and the first bug slow, because they hide the prompts. Start with direct calls; use a framework only if you understand what it does underneath.

**What it means for Exo.** The 3 a.m. jobs are workflows: chaining and routing, cheap and predictable. Only the council and the prep research earn an agent loop, because there the next step really depends on what they find.

## The words

- **Workflow** — steps you wrote, in your order; the model fills in the words
- **Agent** — a model that decides its own steps and loops with tools until done
- **Routing** — classify first, then use the prompt built for that class
- **Evaluator–optimizer** — one model drafts, another judges, and they loop

## Lo que pensó Pablo

terminos.r: steps you wrote, in your order; the model fills in the words
a model that decides its own steps and loops with tools until done
classify first, then use the prompt built for that class
one model drafts, another judges, and they loop

est-goldratt-ferra.nombre: The one constraint at Grupo Ferra
est-goldratt-ferra.texto:
# Goldratt: the one constraint at Grupo Ferra

## Think about this first

If Grupo Ferra's line stopped three times as often tomorrow, what breaks first? Name the step, not the department.

## The 80/20

*The Goal* is a novel about a plant manager with three months to save his plant. The idea under the story fits on a card: every system has one constraint, and the system's output is that constraint's output. Improving anything else is noise until the constraint moves.

**The five focusing steps.**
1. *Identify* the constraint. At Ferra: the supervisor's first 40 minutes after a stoppage, spent writing the report.
2. *Exploit* it: never let the constraint idle. The assistant drafts so the supervisor only approves.
3. *Subordinate* everything else to it. The ERP, the certificates, the CFO's reports queue behind the inbox.
4. *Elevate* it: add capacity only after the first three steps. Not yet.
5. *Repeat*: when the constraint moves, start over. After six weeks it moved to the receiving dock.

**The sentence for the board.** "Supplier emails were the bottleneck; we did not buy a system, we gave the bottleneck an assistant and a rule."

**Where it breaks.** Goldratt measures throughput in money. Ferra's constraint cost hours, not sales, so the board hears "time saved" and asks "and?". The answer is the backlog: 11 days to 1.

## The words

- **Constraint** — the one step that limits the whole system's output
- **Throughput** — the rate at which the system turns inputs into money
- **Subordinate** — make every other step serve the constraint's pace

## Lo que pensó Pablo

terminos.r: the one step that limits the whole system's output
the rate at which the system turns inputs into money
make every other step serve the constraint's pace

est-slope-over-experience.texto:
# Karpathy — Intro to Large Language Models

## Think about this first

If Matthew's founders asked you "what is ChatGPT, really?", what would you say in two sentences?

## The 80/20

**What it is.** A large file of numbers trained to predict the next word. Everything else — answering, writing, reasoning — comes out of doing that one thing very well.

**How it is made.** First it reads a huge slice of the internet (pre-training); then people show it thousands of good conversations so it behaves like an assistant (fine-tuning).

**Why it sometimes makes things up.** It predicts what sounds right, not what it knows is true. That is why Exo always shows its sources from your notes.

**Why it matters for you this week.** Matthew wants someone who can explain AI to engineers without the hype. This is the two-minute version.

## The words

- **Next-token prediction** — what an LLM does: guess the next piece of text, over and over
- **Pre-training vs fine-tuning** — reading the internet to learn language, then examples to learn to be an assistant

## Lo que pensó Pablo

terminos.r: what an LLM does: guess the next piece of text, over and over
reading the internet to learn language, then a smaller set of examples to learn to be an assistant

est-polymaths-reel.texto:
# Paul Graham — Do things that don't scale

## Think about this first

How did you get Grupo Ferra? Write the three things you did by hand.

## The 80/20

**The idea.** Startups don't take off on their own. The founders go out and recruit the first users one by one, and do things for them no big company would.

**The examples.** Airbnb's founders went door to door in New York photographing apartments. Stripe's founders installed the product on people's laptops on the spot.

**Why it matters for you.** Ferra came from sitting with supervisors on the floor, not from a website. The next two clients will come the same way — that is what Outreach is for.

## The words

- **Do things that don't scale** — win the first users by hand, one at a time, before building the machine

## Lo que pensó Pablo

terminos.r: win the first users by hand, one at a time, before building the machine

est-context-windows.texto:
# What a context window is, and why Exo forgets

## Think about this first

When Exo "forgot" the Ferra pricing last week, where was that fact at the moment it answered?

## The 80/20

A context window is everything the model can read at once for one answer. Not in the window, not in the answer. Every agent of Exo starts empty and gets a window filled from files; what the file does not say, the agent cannot know.

## The words

- **Context window** — everything the model can read at once; what is not in it does not exist for that answer

## Lo que pensó Pablo

**Before reading · {{G-12}} 21:10**
I think it forgot because the note was old.

**In my words · {{G-12}} 21:40**
Wrong. It forgot because the note was never in the window. The fix is not a better memory; it is a job that puts the right file in front of the right agent. That is what `sincronia` does, and why the live files exist.

terminos.r: everything the model can read at once; what is not in it does not exist for that answer

est-subsidiarity.texto:
# Subsidiarity as a design rule

## Think about this first

Who decides what the Ferra assistant may answer alone: Daniela, the CFO, or the supervisor?

## The 80/20

Subsidiarity: a decision belongs to the person it lands on; a higher level steps in only when the lower one cannot. As a design rule for AI: ask the most affected, not the most important, and let them set the limits.

## The words

- **Subsidiarity** — a decision belongs to the person it lands on

## Lo que pensó Pablo

**In my words · {{G-9}} 22:05**
The supervisor, and I had it backwards: I was going to ask Daniela. The rule is the answer to her first question, and it is also why the pilot worked: the people on the floor set the limit, so they trusted it.

terminos.r: a decision belongs to the person it lands on
